mem.t: bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, if any man has a complaint against any; even as Christ forgave you, so you also do.

lessons.title: Joseph Forgives His Brothers
lessons.theme: Only when we see God’s hand can we let go of people’s wrongs

v: Joseph said to them, “Don’t be afraid, for am I in the place of God?
As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to save many people alive, as is happening today.
Now therefore don’t be afraid. I will provide for you and your little ones.” He comforted them, and spoke kindly to them.

lessons.still: Think of someone who once hurt you deeply. Don’t rush to forgive; first tell the Lord honestly about the pain. Then ask him to open your eyes to see, behind it all, his hand that has never once let go of you.
teach: The back of a tapestry is a chaotic mess of tangled threads; turn it over, and there is a beautiful picture. Joseph was sold into Egypt by his brothers, thrown into prison on a false charge, and forgotten for years. From the back, it was a tangle of threads. But years later he told his brothers, “You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.”

Notice Joseph’s first words: “Am I in the place of God?” This is the key to forgiveness. Revenge means climbing onto the judgment seat myself and punishing others in God’s place; forgiveness means stepping down from that seat and returning to my place as a human being. Joseph not only refused revenge; he said, “I will provide for you,” and he “comforted them, and spoke kindly to them.”

Joseph did not deny his brothers’ evil — “you meant evil against me,” he said plainly. Forgiveness does not say, “It was nothing.” It says, “It was something, but I hand it over to God.” This week we learn forgiveness and the restoring of relationships — the deepest test of the nine fruits, in relationships that are broken.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Let people be people and let God be God. Unforgiveness is really an expression of the self-ruled life — I want to sit in God’s place and judge. People living the self-emptied life return to their place, and so they can forgive. Humility overcomes pride: Joseph’s forgiveness ended years of hatred among the brothers and saved many lives.
q: Who is God? — “God meant it for good” — in which painful experience have you seen God’s hand?
Who am I? — Are you still sitting on the judgment seat over someone?
How shall I respond? — Are you willing to say to the Lord, “Am I in your place?”
lessons.jesus: Joseph is a foreshadowing of Jesus: betrayed by his brothers, falsely accused, made to suffer, and finally exalted — becoming the saviour of those who betrayed him. Jesus was rejected by his own people and nailed to a cross, yet he became their Saviour, and he prayed, “Father, forgive them.”
lessons.pray: Lord, I confess there are wounds I am still clutching tightly and people I am still judging in my heart. Today I step down from the judgment seat — am I in your place? Help me to see your hand, and give me a forgiving heart, so that I can even speak kindly and bring comfort to those who hurt me. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write down the name of someone you have not yet forgiven, and hand them over to God in prayer
If one of “my 2” has hurt you, pray a prayer of blessing over them today
lessons.noon: “You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” — Lord, right now I trust that your hand is in control.

lessons.title: Seventy Times Seven
lessons.theme: Forgiveness is not a calculation but the way of life of those who have received grace

v: Then Peter came and said to him, “Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Until seven times?”
Jesus said to him, “I don’t tell you until seven times, but, until seventy times seven.
Shouldn’t you also have had mercy on your fellow servant, even as I had mercy on you?’

lessons.still: Quietly recall how many times the Lord has forgiven you. The same sins, the same weaknesses — you have come back to him again and again, and he has never once said, “That’s enough.” Let this grace slowly soak into your heart.
teach: Peter thought he was being very generous: “Until seven times?” Seven is the number of completeness. But Jesus said, “I don’t tell you until seven times, but, until seventy times seven.” He did not mean that on the four hundred and ninety-first time we may stop forgiving; he meant that forgiveness is not something to count at all.

Then Jesus told a parable. A servant owed his master ten thousand talents, and the master cancelled the whole debt. But the servant went out, seized a fellow servant who owed him a hundred denarii by the throat, and refused to show him mercy. The master said, “Shouldn’t you also have had mercy on your fellow servant, even as I had mercy on you?” The root of the problem was this: he had forgotten how much he had been forgiven.

We refuse to forgive because we make others’ debts too big and our own too small. A change of mindset: I am someone who has been forgiven ten thousand talents. When I remember the grace of the cross, forgiving someone else’s hundred denarii is no longer a heavy command but the natural overflow of gratitude.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Change your mindset and you change your life. Self-ruled people keep accounts of what others owe them; people living the self-emptied life keep count of grace — what God has forgiven them. Forgiveness does not come from self-improvement; it is the life of Christ flowing naturally from those who live the self-emptied life.
q: Who is God? — The master cancelled ten thousand talents — what does that show you about God’s heart?
Who am I? — Whose account are you still keeping in your heart?
How shall I respond? — How will you remember every day the grace of being forgiven?
lessons.jesus: Jesus did not only teach forgiveness; he himself is the Master who cancelled our debt of ten thousand talents. On the cross he paid our debt in full, and he welcomes those who turn back to him again and again. It is precisely because he forgave us first that we have the strength to forgive others.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for cancelling my debt of ten thousand talents and forgiving me again and again. Forgive me for so often remembering others’ hundred denarii while forgetting the grace you have given me. Today I choose to stop keeping accounts, and to have mercy on my fellow servants as you have had mercy on me. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write down three things God has forgiven you for, and give thanks for them
Hand over to the Lord an offence you keep replaying in your mind, and stop replaying it
Forgive one of “my 2” for a small thing, and never bring it up again
lessons.noon: “I don’t tell you until seven times, but, until seventy times seven.” — Lord, right now I remember your forgiveness of me.

lessons.title: Forgiving Is Not Forgetting
lessons.theme: Forgiveness hands judgment over to God; it does not pretend we were never hurt

v: I, even I, am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake; and I will not remember your sins.
When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously.

lessons.still: If forgiveness is still hard for you, don’t blame yourself. Quietly lay your wound open before the Lord and say, “Lord, it still hurts, but I am willing to hand judgment over to you.” Let the Lord lay his hand on the wound.
teach: When a wound heals, it may still leave a scar. Seeing the scar doesn’t mean the wound is still bleeding. Many people think that “forgiving means forgetting,” so every time they recall the past they blame themselves: “I still remember — does that mean I haven’t forgiven?” But memory is not the same as resentment, just as a scar is not the same as a wound.

God says, “I will not remember your sins.” The all-knowing God has not lost his memory; he has chosen not to hold these sins against us any more. Peter says that when Jesus suffered, he “committed himself to him who judges righteously.” That is what forgiveness is: I don’t deny that I was hurt, but I give up my right to collect the debt, and I entrust justice to God.

Forgiveness is also not the same as immediately restoring trust. Forgiveness is a one-sided decision that can begin today; trust is rebuilt by both sides over time, and it needs fruit. A change of mindset: forgiveness does not say, “You did nothing wrong.” It says, “I no longer require you to repay me” — I hand you over to God, and I set myself free from bitterness.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Focus on Jesus — not on others, and not on our own wounds. Handing judgment over to God is returning to our place; only when I let God be God am I set free. Replaying the past in the head brings only worry; living from the heart by the Spirit brings healing from bitterness.
q: Who is God? — God “will not remember” our sins — what kind of grace is that?
Who am I? — Have you mistaken “I still remember” for “I haven’t forgiven yet”?
How shall I respond? — Which debt are you willing to hand over to him who judges righteously?
lessons.jesus: After his resurrection, Jesus still bore the nail marks in his hands and the wound in his side. He did not erase the scars; he made them the grounds for Thomas’s faith. In Jesus’ hands, our scars too can turn from marks of shame into testimonies of grace.
lessons.pray: Lord who judges righteously, I hand over to you my pain and my right to collect the debt. I won’t pretend I was never hurt, but I choose not to hold on to resentment. Heal my wounds and make my scars a testimony to your grace, and give me wisdom to know how to rebuild the relationship. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write: “I forgive ____, and I hand them over to God.”
When the past comes back to mind, pray once instead of replaying it once
Let go of an old grievance against one of “my 2,” and stop dragging it back up
lessons.noon: “But committed himself to him who judges righteously.” — Lord, right now I hand judgment over to you.

lessons.title: Taking the First Step to Restore
lessons.theme: Don’t wait for the other person to come first; Jesus tells us to go

v: “If therefore you are offering your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has anything against you,
leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.
“If your brother sins against you, go, show him his fault between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained back your brother.

lessons.still: Ask the Holy Spirit to bring to mind a relationship that has a crack in it — perhaps you wronged someone, perhaps someone wronged you. Don’t rush to work out who was right and who was wrong; simply ask, “Lord, what small step do you want me to take?”
teach: When a river freezes over, someone has to break the first crack in the ice. When a relationship breaks down, we often wait — for the other person to apologise first, to call first, to back down first. But Jesus gives two scenarios, and the answer to both is the same: “You go.”

In the first scenario, you have wronged someone: “if you… remember that your brother has anything against you,” even worship must pause — “first be reconciled to your brother.” In the second, someone has wronged you: “go, show him his fault between you and him alone.” Whoever is right or wrong, the one who takes the initiative is “you.” The goal is not to win but to have “gained back your brother.”

Restoring a relationship takes wisdom: speak privately, without public shaming; speak about facts, without attacking character; aim to win the person, not to prove yourself right. Sometimes the other person won’t respond, and even so we have done our part. A change of mindset: taking the first step is not losing; it is letting Jesus reign in this relationship.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility is the key to revival. Pride waits for the other person to back down first; humility goes and knocks on the door first. Humility draws out humility and both sides win — the one who takes the first step towards reconciliation often opens the other person’s heart. First with God, then with others; being reconciled with others is part of our fellowship with God.
q: Who is God? — God came to reconcile us to himself while we were still his enemies — what does that show you about him?
Who am I? — In which relationship have you been “waiting for the other person to come first”?
How shall I respond? — Towards whom will you take the first step of restoration?
lessons.jesus: While we were still God’s enemies, Jesus took the initiative and came into the world, reconciling us to God through the cross (Romans 5:10). He did not wait for us to apologise first; he paid the price of reconciliation first, and then entrusted to us the ministry of reconciliation. The initiative to reconcile has always been on God’s side.
lessons.pray: Lord, you came first to be reconciled with me, yet I often wait for others to come to me first. Give me humility and courage to take the first step towards that broken relationship. Give me fitting words, so that I seek not to win but to gain back my brother or sister. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Send a message to one of “my 2,” taking the first step to break a chill between you
If you have wronged someone, go and apologise today — with no “but” attached
Pray first for the conversation to restore the relationship, and write down the first sentence you will say
lessons.noon: “First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.” — Lord, right now give me courage to take the first step.

lessons.title: Don’t Hurt People over Things
lessons.theme: Christ died for each person; people are more precious than any task

v: Yet if because of food your brother is grieved, you walk no longer in love. Don’t destroy with your food him for whom Christ died.
So then, let’s follow after things which make for peace, and things by which we may build one another up.

lessons.still: Recall a recent “thing” that put you in conflict with someone: a plan, an opinion, a way of doing things. Put it in your left hand; put that person in your right hand. Quietly ask the Lord, “Lord, in your eyes, which weighs more?”
teach: A parent yells at a child over a broken vase. The vase cannot be saved, and now the child’s heart is broken too. We often hurt people over things: over a meeting’s decision, a ministry procedure, who was right and who was wrong. The task gets done, but the person walks away. This week we have walked through Joseph’s forgiveness (Day 1), seventy times seven (Day 2), forgiving is not forgetting (Day 3), and taking the first step to restore (Day 4).

The early church argued fiercely over “what to eat.” Paul did not begin by ruling on who was right. He said, “Don’t destroy with your food him for whom Christ died.” That sentence turns the whole matter’s weight upside down — food is a thing, but a brother is a person bought with Christ’s life. So “let’s follow after things which make for peace, and things by which we may build one another up.”

This does not mean tasks are unimportant; it means tasks should serve people, not people be sacrificed for tasks. Next week we will learn about the rhythm of family and work — exactly the place where it is easiest to hurt people over things. A change of mindset: before doing anything, ask, “Will this build people up, or hurt them?”
lessons.light: 321 Light: People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things; don’t hurt people over things. Life first, then relationships, then ministry — if ministry damages relationships, it has lost its meaning. God’s kingdom system is built on people who are loved, not on tasks that are completed.
q: Who is God? — “Him for whom Christ died” — how does this change the way you see the person nearby who gives you headaches?
Who am I? — Have you recently hurt someone over some task or issue?
How shall I respond? — How will you put people back in the place where they weigh more than things?
lessons.jesus: On his way to save Jairus’s daughter, Jesus still stopped to seek out, listen to and bless a woman who had suffered from bleeding. He stopped for a blind man crying out by the roadside, and changed his plans for Zacchaeus in the tree. To him, people always mattered more than tasks.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, forgive me for so often hurting people over things, and losing brothers and sisters over who was right. Thank you for laying down your life for every person. Help me to see people as you see them, to love people before doing tasks, and to build people up before insisting on my way. I want to pursue the things that make for peace. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Sincerely apologise to one of “my 2” for a time you hurt them over some task or issue
Before your next meeting or decision, first pray for the people involved
Tomorrow (Saturday), share this week’s lessons on forgiveness with your spiritual companion
lessons.noon: “Let’s follow after things which make for peace, and things by which we may build one another up.” — Lord, right now let me put people before things.
